lines: Rethinking Credit Assignment in Cooperative MARL
Credit assignment remains a central challenge in cooperative multi-agent reinforce-
ment learning (MARL), especially under partial observability, where individual
policy updates may not accurately reflect each agent’s actual contribution to team
outcomes. While policy-based methods such as MAPPO and IPPO provide strong
optimization frameworks, their updates are typically derived from global rewards
and observational value surrogates, without explicitly defining agent-specific credit.
Misaligned credit signals can misguide individual policy improvement, resulting
in inefficient coordination and weaker team performance. We address this chal-
lenge by formulating agent-level credit as an interventional reward response, using
Proximal Causal Inference (PCI) to identify credit from observable proxies via
an outcome bridge function. Building on this identification strategy, we design a
practical credit-aligned update signal and integrate it into policy gradient meth-
ods. Empirical evaluations on diagnostic and benchmark tasks demonstrate that
the proposed credit signal improves policy learning under partial observability,
highlighting proximal identification as a promising foundation for designing credit-
aware policy updates in cooperative MARL. To the best of our knowledge, this
work presents the first PCI-based solution for online multi-agent cooperation.
Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) studies how multiple agents learn to coordi-
nate toward a shared objective under local views of the environment. Such settings capture a core
issue in control of complex systems, including multi-robot coordination [38], traffic signal control
[35], and large-scale resource allocation in communication networks [42], where multiple agents
Despite notable success across benchmark tasks, standard policy-based approaches still rely on update
signals constructed from shared global rewards and observational value surrogates [4, 9]. These
signals often fail to align with each agent’s actual contribution to team outcomes [34, 40]. This
issue becomes more pronounced under partial observability, where local observations alone may
not sufficiently capture the decision context. Misaligned signals ultimately hinder efficient policy
improvement, leading to suboptimal policies or slower convergence [8, 44]. Existing approaches
enhance coordination through value decomposition [25, 31], centralized critics [39], or counterfactual
baselines [8], but they do not fully accommodate agent-specific credit through an interventional
reward target. That is, they do not explicitly capture the effect of the action changes of a focal agent
This mismatch is especially pronounced when the reward-generation mechanism is not exchange-

compatibility with others. In such cases, the shared global reward can remain informative about
collective performance while still being highly ambiguous about which agent’s action actually con-
tributed to that outcome. This makes agent-wise credit assignment fundamentally interventional
rather than something that can be resolved from shared reward alone. To resolve this issue, we
define agent-specific credit as intervention. In a decentralized partially observable Markov deci-
sion process (Dec-POMDP), the realized global reward is generated by the unobserved underlying
state and the joint action. Consequently, the observed reward alone does not reveal how the team
outcome would change if a single agent’s action changes [22]. This motivates defining agent-wise
credit via an interventional reward response—how the global reward responds to intervening on the
agent’s action—rather than relying solely on observational reward associations. To operationalize this
perspective, we leverage Proximal Causal Inference (PCI; [19, 32]), a principled framework for iden-
tifying interventional reward responses from observable proxy variables when the reward-generating
state is not observed. Within the Dec-POMDP setting, we instantiate agent-specific proxies and
identify the target interventional reward through an outcome bridge function.
• Interventional Credit: We formulate agent-specific credit under partial observability as an inter-
ventional reward response and a corresponding contrastive credit quantity.
• PCI-based identification: We develop a PCI-based framework in Dec-POMDPs that identifies
the interventional reward response through an outcome bridge function and operationalizes it as a
practical credit-aligned update signal for online policy-based cooperative MARL.
• Empirical Validation: We empirically validate the method on diagnostic and benchmark domains,
demonstrating improved policy learning over MAPPO/IPPO backbones and verifying the behavior
of the learned outcome bridge and credit-aligned reward.
Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning. Representative cooperative MARL methods include value-
factorization approaches such as VDN [31] and QMIX [25], as well as PPO-based baselines such as
MAPPO [39] and IPPO [5]. These methods achieve strong empirical performance, but still learn from
shared team rewards and rollout-based value surrogates rather than explicitly defining agent-wise
credit. COMA [8] introduces a counterfactual baseline for multi-agent credit assignment, yet it
still relies on the observed global reward signal. In contrast, we formulate agent-wise credit as an
interventional target and identify it through a proxy-based causal framework.
Causal Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning. Recent research has sought to integrate causal
inference methods with the powerful learning methods of RL, a line of work referred to as causal re-
inforcement learning (CRL) [1, 16]. CRL studies how intervention semantics, structural assumptions,
or causal representations can improve policy learning, robustness, or interpretability in sequential
decision-making. Most CRL studies focus on single-agent settings, including causal imitation and
confounding-aware offline RL [13, 41]. In multi-agent systems, however, explicit causal treatments
of credit assignment remain relatively limited. The approaches closest to ours are deconfounded value
decomposition (DVD) [15] and its follow-up studies [17, 37]. Our work differs in both target and
methodology: rather than modifying the value decomposition, we focus on identifying agent-wise
credit through an interventional reward target under partial observability.
Reinforcement Learning with Proximal Causal Inference. The most relevant prior works extend
PCI to sequential decision-making within a single-agent domain. Bennett and Kallus [3] tackle
off-policy evaluation in a partially observable MDP (POMDP) framework by developing proximal
identification strategies for applications of offline RL to observational data. Hong et al. [10] proposes
a policy gradient method that identifies causal policy gradients under hidden confounders in offline
settings. Shen and Cui [30] focuses on the learning of optimal individualized treatment regimes
(ITRs) for efficient estimation of a value function. These works predominantly focus on offline or
off-policy settings motivated by observational domains such as healthcare, rather than cooperative
MARL training. To the best of our knowledge, prior PCI-based sequential decision-making works
have not treated practical cooperative MARL training as the primary setting. In contrast, we use PCI
to identify agent-wise credit and turn it into a practical update signal for cooperative MARL training.

Intervention in Causal Inference. Causal inference is the process of understanding the independent
and genuine impact of a particular variable within a complex system. The pivotal constructs of causal
inference encompass association and intervention. An association is an observational relationship
in which correlations between variables are observed without causal manipulation. An intervention
involves deliberately manipulating a variable while severing all incoming pathways directed toward
it, leaving the rest of the system unchanged, thereby facilitating the examination of its influence
on an outcome. To introduce interventions within the Dec-POMDP causal graph (Figure 1), we
adopt Pearl’s do-operator [24, Section 1.3.1], where an intervention on agent i’s action is denoted
intervention that overrides only agent i’s action at time t, while the environment dynamics and other
agents’ actions continue to follow the Dec-POMDP mechanism (their decentralized policies).

4 Credit Assignment Requires an Interventional View
In Dec-POMDPs, the global reward is determined by a function of the unobserved state and the joint
action, and the same reward is given to all agents. Therefore, the realized global reward conflates
the influences of the unobserved state and the actions of all agents, creating structural ambiguity
for agent-wise credit assignment. In standard cooperative policy-based MARL, the shared global
reward is used to construct individual update signals, such as value or advantage estimates. Although
such shared update signals are effective for optimization, they do not explicitly isolate each agent’s
contribution to the team outcome [36]. Prior work has shown that learning from the global reward
under partial observability can induce spurious rewards [8] and the lazy-agent problem [31], and
more generally make it difficult for each agent to infer its own contribution to the team outcome [44].
4.2 Agent-specific Credit Assignment Via Interventional Reward Response
What is missing, then, is not the team objective itself, but a principled agent-wise target for translating
that shared reward into individual credit. The key question for agent-wise credit is how the global
reward would change if the focal agent’s action were changed under the same decision situation. We
refer to this fixed information available before the decision-making as the pre-action context. In
other words, credit should be assigned to an action for its effect on the global reward, rather than for
being merely associated with a realized reward. This is inherently a causal question, which motivates
defining agent-wise credit through an interventional reward response rather than relying solely on
realized global rewards and observational value surrogates.

7.1 A Diagnostic Stag-Hunt Benchmark for Agent-Wise Credit Assignment
The classical Stag-Hunt game captures the tension between safe individual behavior and high-payoff
coordination. To make this structure more suitable for studying agent-wise credit assignment under
partial observability, we introduce a diagnostic Stag-Hunt benchmark. The environment is a partially
observable grid-world with an equal number of agents, hares, and stags. Each hare can be captured
individually for a small reward (+3). In contrast, each stag i can be captured only through successful
coordination between a designated pair of agents (i, i + 1) (with wrap-around, Figure F.1), yielding
a larger reward (+5). This rule induces a non-exchangeable contribution structure: successful
trajectories can contain many actions correlated with the observed team outcome, while only a
specific coordination is actually reward-generating for a given stag. All agents receive the same
shared team reward, so the cooperative objective is preserved while individual contribution ambiguity
is made explicit. Additional environmental details are provided in Appendix F.
Figure 2a reports the learning curves. Our methods (PCI-IPPO and PCI-MAPPO) outperform
their counterparts’ backbones that use raw shared global reward as the policy update signal. Both
reach approximately 80% success rate at the end of training, while IPPO and MAPPO plateau at
roughly 40% and 70%, respectively. A particularly informative comparison is between PCI-IPPO
and MAPPO: MAPPO conditions its critic on global information under the CTDE paradigm, yet
PCI-IPPO achieves superior performance. This suggests that the centralized critic information alone
may not fully resolve the credit-assignment bottleneck. In contrast, the PCI-based correction is
constructed from an explicitly interventional notion of agent-wise credit. To test robustness under
partial observability, we add white Gaussian noise to observations. The second plot in Figure 2a
reports that our methods maintain approximately 50-60% success rate, whereas baselines fall near or
below 20%. The noisy observations conceal the underlying state, thereby making it harder to attribute
the global reward correctly from observational signals alone. PCI-based methods are more robust in

three cases are clearly separated during training. In the Stag case, the normalized signal remains

To complement the diagnostic Stag-Hunt domain, we evaluate our methods under SMAX [26]
benchmark with target-allocation constraints. Each agent i is assigned an admissible target set Ti,
and an attack on enemy e is effective only if e ∈ Ti; otherwise, it nullifies allied attacks on that
target. This preserves the original cooperative objective while making agent-wise credit contrast more
explicit, so we use the SMAX-variant as a controlled diagnostic setting rather than a replacement for
the original benchmark. The strength of the restriction is governed by |Ti|: Medium corresponds to
roughly 80% target availability and Hard to 50–80%.
Table 2 reports the average test win rates over six SMAX maps covering both SMAC [27] and
SMACv2 [7] scenarios. Across all constraint levels, PCI-based methods improve over their corre-
sponding backbones on average. More importantly, the improvement becomes substantially larger
as the target-allocation constraint is strengthened. For IPPO, the gain increases from +2.8% in the
Vanilla setting to +11.6% in Medium and +27.8% in Hard; for MAPPO, the corresponding gains are
+4.5%, +9.1%, and +10.5%. This pattern is consistent with our hypothesis: as the admissible target
sets shrink, the reward-generation mechanism becomes less exchangeable across agents, and the mis-
match between shared reward and agent-wise actual contribution becomes more severe. In this regime,
the advantage of explicitly estimating interventional credit becomes more pronounced. The average
improvements under the Vanilla setting are also notable. Even without the target-allocation constraint,
PCI-IPPO/-MAPPO outperform their respective baselines, suggesting that standard SMAX already
contains nontrivial agent-wise credit ambiguity. At the same time, the larger gains under Medium
and Hard indicate that the SMAX-variant does not merely make the task harder; rather, it selectively
amplifies the aspect of the problem targeted by our method, namely the discrepancy between shared
team reward and agent-wise interventional contribution. Although the training curves sometimes
show slower convergence or weak performances on some scenarios (Figure F.3), final-checkpoint
evaluation over 64 random seeds still yields average improvements. Compared with Stag-Hunt
domain, SMAX presents a denser and more complex reward structure, with less explicit coordination
boundaries. The fact that PCI-based improvements persist in this setting suggests that the proposed
approach is not limited to sparse-reward or highly stylized coordination tasks. Instead, the results
indicate that correcting policy updates with an interventional credit signal remains beneficial even
when the environment provides richer but more entangled feedback.

Summary. We studied agent-wise credit assignment in cooperative MARL through an interventional
lens and argued that global rewards and observational value surrogates do not directly capture
individual contribution under partial observability. To this end, we formulated agent-wise credit
through an interventional reward response and the resulting credit contrast, and showed that the
interventional reward response can be identified from observational trajectories via PCI. Building
on this, we developed a practical method that learns an outcome bridge and uses a bridge-based
counterfactual baseline for credit-aligned individual policy updates. Empirically, our method improves
policy learning in the custom Stag-Hunt domain and SMAX benchmark, suggesting that the learned
bridge and shaped reward capture meaningful agent-wise credit.
Limitations. Our approach has several limitations. First, the identification results rely on the
validity of the action-side and outcome-side proxies. If these assumptions are only approximate, the
learned bridge may fail to recover the interventional reward response accurately, biasing the resulting
credit signal. Second, our method assumes that a suitable outcome bridge exists and can be well
approximated by the chosen function class. Finite-sample effects, optimization error, and model
misspecification may degrade bridge estimation, especially when the proxies are weak. Third, the
practical effectiveness of the method depends on the backbone RL framework and the quality of its
t and the proxies rely on RNN-encoded histories. Furthermore, the
method inherits limitations of the underlying backbone and remains suboptimal on some SMAX
scenarios that the backbone itself struggles to solve (Table F.2).

The minimax approach to reformulate the conditional moment restriction has been established via
various studies in recent years [6, 14]. The rationale behind the connection between conditional
moment restriction and minimax reformulation lies in the law of iterated expectations. For the
outcome bridge function h, the conditional moment restriction is given by,
E[Y − h(W, A, X)|Z, A, X] = 0.
Here, we suppose all variables and functions are scalar for simplicity. By definition, this conditional
expectation is zero if and only if the unconditional expectation is zero for any square-integrable test
function (or critic function) q ∈ L2(Z, A, X). This equivalence allows us to reformulate the problem
as finding a function h that minimizes the maximum violation of these unconditional moments across

While this forms the basis of the adversarial generalized method of moments (AGMM), directly
optimizing this squared objective can be highly unstable in practice. To address this, a stabilizer
term is introduced. For any constant λ > 0, the squared conditional expectation can be exactly
reformulated as a penalized supremum problem,

bounds the norm of the critic function, thereby controlling the critical radius of the function class.

The Stag-Hunt environment is a 7 × 7 partially observable grid-
world containing an equal number N of agents, hares, and stags.
Each hare can be captured individually for a small reward (+3).
If multiple agents attempt to capture the same hare, the reward
is allocated to a randomly selected agent. Each stag i can be cap-
tured only through successful coordination between a designated
pair of agents (i, i + 1) (with wrap-around), yielding a larger
reward (+5). At each timestep, every agent receives a 5 × 5 local
observation represented as a multi-channel boolean tensor that
encodes the positions of entities and boundaries. Each boolean
channel indicates the presence of the i-th stag, the i-th agent, or
a hare. Unlike stags and agents, hares are not uniquely identified.
Consequently, the boolean channel vector for each grid cell has
a length of 2N + 1. For our specific scenario with N = 3 agents,
this results in a channel vector length of 7 per cell. Given the
5 × 5 local observation grid, the flattened observation dimension for each agent is 175. Any grid cell
falling outside the environment boundaries is masked with a value of -1 across all channels.
